deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page): L(y)=y'''+p1 y''+p2 y'+p3 y=0 is a third-order linear ODE. The functions y1, y2, y3 form a fundamental system. Hilbert sets up
  D(x;u) = det[[y1,y1',u1],[y2,y2',u2],[y3,y3',u3]] = 0.
Expanding along the last column gives D = u·(y × y'), where y=(y1,y2,y3) [expansion mine]. For fixed x this equation is linear in u. Read projectively in the plane of (y1:y2:y3), it is the tangent line at the point y(x) to the integral curve x ↦ (y1(x):y2(x):y3(x)) [geometric reading mine].

This page, part 1: the single equation D(x;u)=0 relates x to the two ratios u1/u2 and u3/u2. Solving it for x ('Umkehrung') gives x = φ(u1/u2, u3/u2). This is a function of two variables. Its value at a point u is the parameter of the curve point whose tangent passes through u. In general it is multivalued, since several tangents pass through a point.

Hilbert's claim is that φ is unchanged under certain linear fractional transformations of u1:u2:u3, namely those of the group (monodromy group) of the ODE.
Verification [mine]: continuation along a loop sends y to M y with M in GL3(C), and likewise y' to M y'. Then
  det[M y, M y', u] = det M · det[y, y', M^{-1} u].
So the continued equation at u is equivalent to the original equation at M^{-1}u. Hence φ(M^{-1}u) agrees, up to choice of branch, with the continued φ(u). In other words, φ is automorphic under the projective monodromy group acting on the point u.

This is the 3rd-order, two-variable analogue of inverting the Schwarzian ratio y1/y2 for a 2nd-order equation. Hilbert compares it with Picard's functions of two variables (hyperfuchsian / hyperabelian functions, c. 1881-85). Those serve to parametrize ('lösen') an algebraic relation f(x,y,z)=0, i.e. to uniformize an algebraic surface.

Part 2 (a question, continued on the next page). Are all finite groups of linear transformations in any number of variables holoedrically (faithfully) isomorphic to a group of linear fractional substitutions in one variable, z ↦ (az+b)/(cz+d)? The coefficients are to be taken modulo a suitable module system (an ideal) of integral polynomials with integer coefficients. Equivalently: does every finite group embed in PGL2(R) for some quotient ring R = Z[t1,...,tk]/M ('Congruenzgruppe mit einer Veränderlichen')?

The next page begins a proof strategy: first conjugate the group so that all matrix entries lie in a cyclotomic field. Then reduce modulo a suitable ideal.
errors: Grammar slip: 'eine Funktion x ..., welche ... ungeändert bleiben' (should be 'bleibt'); immaterial.

The inversion x = φ(u1/u2, u3/u2) is in general multivalued, since a point lies on several tangents of the integral curve. The invariance therefore holds only up to branch. Hilbert does not address single-valuedness, which is needed for a genuine automorphic function (cf. Picard's conditions).
The precise action is u ↦ M^{-1}u, the monodromy group itself acting on points; the sign or inverse convention is left implicit. This is harmless since a group is closed under inverses.

The question in part 2 appears to have a negative answer in general (my analysis, moderate confidence). For a finitely generated commutative ring R, a finite subgroup of PGL2(R) survives in PGL2 of some finite quotient ring. A finite ring is a product of local rings, and over a finite local ring the kernel of reduction to the residue field is a p-group. Hence every non-abelian simple composition factor of such a group is a PSL2(q). So, for example, A7 cannot be faithfully represented this way. Hilbert poses it only as a question ('?'), so this is an unsettled query rather than an asserted error.

results.what: Defining a two-variable function automorphic under the monodromy group of a 3rd-order linear ODE, by inverting the tangent-line equation det[y,y',u]=0.
results.modern_name: Generalized Schwarz map / automorphic (hyperfuchsian-type) functions of two variables attached to a third-order Fuchsian equation; inversion of the developing map.
results.usually_credited_to: Analogue of Schwarz (1873) and Klein for 2nd order. For 3rd order and two variables: Fuchs (c.1880, inversion problems), Halphen, Picard (1881-85 hyperfuchsian functions), later Klein's lectures on linear ODEs (1890s) and Appell-Lauricella/Picard work.

results.what: Question whether every finite linear group is isomorphic to a group of linear fractional substitutions in one variable over a quotient ring Z[t]/M.
results.modern_name: Embedding finite groups into PGL2 over finite (or finitely generated) commutative rings; congruence (reduction mod ideal) representations.
results.usually_credited_to: Related to work on finite subgroups of PSL2 / PGL2 over finite fields (Moore, Dickson 1890s-1901) and modular congruence groups (Klein, Gierster). The question itself is not known to be credited to anyone.

deep.surprise_reason: Part 1 is a standard 1880s construction (Fuchs/Picard/Klein milieu) and Hilbert explicitly cites Picard. Part 2 is an interesting unpublished research question, apparently with a negative answer. The cyclotomic-coefficient idea on the next page foreshadows Schur/Brauer, but this page only poses the question. It is a notable note-to-self, not a result.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x=symbols('x'); y=Matrix([Function('y%d'%i)(x) for i in (1,2,3)]); u=Matrix(symbols('u1:4')); M=Matrix(3,3,symbols('m1:10')); lhs=Matrix.hstack(M*y,M*y.diff(x),u).det(); rhs=M.det()*Matrix.hstack(y,y.diff(x),M.inv()*u).det(); simplify(lhs-rhs)==0
checkable.asserts: Under monodromy y -> M y, the tangent-line equation at u becomes the original one at M^{-1}u. So x(u) is invariant (up to branch) under the projective monodromy group.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x=symbols('x'); y=Matrix([Function('y%d'%i)(x) for i in (1,2,3)]); u=Matrix(symbols('u1:4')); simplify(Matrix.hstack(y,y.diff(x),u).det() - u.dot(y.cross(y.diff(x))))==0
checkable.asserts: The determinant is linear in u and equals u·(y × y'), i.e. it is the tangent line to the curve (y1:y2:y3) at parameter x.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; q=symbols('q',integer=True,positive=True); [qq for qq in range(2,200) if isprime(factorint(qq) and list(factorint(qq).keys())[0]) and len(factorint(qq))==1 and qq*(qq**2-1)//gcd(2,qq-1)==2520]
checkable.asserts: No prime power q has |PSL2(q)| = 2520 = |A7| (empty list). This supports, together with the structural argument, that A7 is not a PSL2(q), relevant to the negative answer to the part-2 question.
